lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Plant Parts and Their Agricultural Uses

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Identify plant parts that are used for agricultural purposes.
- Describe how plant parts are used for agricultural purposes.
- List the uses of plant parts for agricultural purposes, such as planting, tools, animal housing, animal feed, soil improvement, and pest and disease control.

pages.title: Roots Used for Agricultural Purposes
pages.body: Roots, beyond their role in the living plant, can be used agriculturally for planting, since certain root cuttings, such as cassava stems with attached root nodes, are used to propagate new crops directly, and for soil improvement, since the roots of leguminous plants, studied in an earlier strand, support nitrogen fixation that enriches soil for subsequent crops.

pages.title: Stems Used for Agricultural Purposes
pages.body: Stems are used agriculturally in several ways, including as planting material, since sugarcane and cassava are both commonly propagated from stem cuttings rather than seeds, as tool making material, since bamboo and certain hardwood stems are shaped into handles for hoes, rakes and other simple agricultural tools studied in an earlier strand, and as animal feed, since maize stalks and other crop stems remaining after harvest are commonly fed to ruminant animals, also studied earlier.

pages.title: Leaves Used for Agricultural Purposes
pages.body: Leaves serve several agricultural purposes, including as animal feed, since cassava leaves, groundnut leaves and various fodder crops are fed directly to livestock, as soil improvement material, since fallen leaves decompose into manure, studied in an earlier strand, and as natural pest control, since certain leaves, such as neem leaves, contain compounds that can repel or control specific agricultural pests when processed and applied appropriately.

pages.title: Flowers Used for Agricultural Purposes
pages.body: Flowers play a specific agricultural role in supporting pollination, since flowering plants attract bees and other pollinating insects essential for the reproduction of many food crops, and some flowers are cultivated specifically to attract beneficial insects to a farm, a practice sometimes called companion planting, which can help support natural pest control and improve pollination rates for nearby food crops.

pages.title: Fruits Used for Agricultural Purposes
pages.body:
Fruits serve agricultural purposes beyond direct human consumption, including as a source of seeds for planting future crops, since many fruits contain the seeds needed to grow the next generation of that same plant, and as animal feed, since fruit that is unsuitable for human consumption, due to blemishes or overripeness, can still be fed to livestock rather than wasted.

[[pic:A labelled diagram of a single plant, with callout boxes pointing to each part (root, stem, leaf, flower, fruit), each callout listing a specific agricultural use, roots for propagation and soil improvement, stems for planting material, tools and feed, leaves for feed, manure and pest control, flowers for pollination support, and fruit for seed source and feed.]]

Notice how a single plant can contribute agricultural value through nearly every one of its parts, rather than only through the specific part typically harvested for food, illustrating how thoroughly useful a well understood plant can be within a farming system.

pages.title: Categorising Agricultural Uses of Plant Parts
pages.body: Planting material, tool making material, animal housing material, animal feed, soil improvement material, and pest and disease control material are six broad categories capturing the range of agricultural uses plant parts serve. Recognising these categories helps farmers think systematically about how to make full, efficient use of the plants grown or available on their farm, rather than overlooking valuable secondary uses beyond the primary harvested crop.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Bamboo and palm fronds, in addition to their tool making uses already discussed, are also widely used across many Ghanaian farming communities to construct simple animal housing structures, such as chicken coops or goat pens, demonstrating yet another agricultural use of plant stems and leaves beyond feed, tools and soil improvement.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Plant Parts and Their Nonagricultural Uses

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Identify plant parts that are used for nonagricultural purposes.
- Describe how plant parts are used for nonagricultural purposes.
- List the uses of plant parts for nonagricultural purposes, such as herbal medicine, construction of houses, bridges and furniture, artefacts, ceremonies, rituals, and education.

pages.title: Roots Used for Nonagricultural Purposes
pages.body: Certain plant roots are valued in herbal medicine, since specific roots contain natural chemical compounds believed, and in some cases scientifically confirmed, to have medicinal properties used in treating various ailments within traditional healing practices. Some roots are also carved or shaped into small decorative or ceremonial artefacts, valued for their unusual natural shapes or cultural significance.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a nonagricultural use of plant roots?
questions.e: Roots Used for Nonagricultural Purposes Certain plant roots are valued in herbal medicine, since specific roots contain natural chemical compounds believed, and in some cases scientifically confirmed, to have medicinal properties…

pages.title: Stems Used for Nonagricultural Purposes
pages.body: Wood from tree stems, or trunks, is a fundamental nonagricultural construction material, used to build houses, bridges, and furniture across many communities, valued for its strength, availability, and workability. Bamboo stems, beyond their agricultural uses discussed in the previous lesson, are also widely used nonagriculturally in scaffolding, furniture making, and even in some traditional musical instruments.

pages.title: Leaves Used for Nonagricultural Purposes
pages.body: Certain leaves are used in traditional herbal medicine, prepared as teas, poultices or extracts believed to treat specific ailments, while others, such as broad palm or plantain leaves, are traditionally used for wrapping food, roofing simple structures, or as part of certain ceremonial and ritual practices within specific cultural traditions.

pages.title: Flowers Used for Nonagricultural Purposes
pages.body: Flowers are commonly used decoratively, in ceremonies such as weddings and funerals, and in some cultural and religious rituals where specific flowers carry particular symbolic meaning. Certain flowers are also used in traditional medicine, and some are processed to extract fragrant oils used in perfumes and other scented products.

pages.title: Fruits Used for Nonagricultural Purposes
pages.body:
Certain fruits and their shells or husks are used to make artefacts, such as carved calabash bowls and containers, while others are used in traditional medicine, valued for specific compounds believed to have health benefits. Some fruits also feature prominently in specific cultural ceremonies and rituals, carrying symbolic meaning beyond their nutritional value.

[[pic:A labelled diagram of the same plant used in the previous lesson, but this time with callout boxes showing nonagricultural uses, roots and leaves used for herbal medicine, stems used for house and furniture construction, flowers used in ceremonies, and fruit shells carved into artefacts, with a small icon representing each use.]]

Notice how the very same plant parts studied for their agricultural value in the previous lesson can serve an entirely different, equally important set of nonagricultural purposes, illustrating how thoroughly a single plant can be understood and valued within a community.

pages.title: Categorising Nonagricultural Uses of Plant Parts
pages.body: Herbal medicine, construction (houses, bridges and furniture), artefacts, ceremonies and rituals, and education are five broad categories capturing the range of nonagricultural uses plant parts serve. The educational category includes using plant parts as teaching specimens in schools, helping learners directly observe and study plant structure, exactly as this reading notes book has encouraged throughout earlier strands covering plant biology.

pages.title: Cultural Significance of Plant Based Ceremonies and Rituals
pages.body: Many communities in Ghana and beyond attach specific cultural or spiritual significance to certain plants or plant parts, using them in naming ceremonies, funerals, festivals, and other important community events, reflecting a deep, longstanding relationship between plant knowledge and cultural identity that extends well beyond the plant's practical, physical uses alone.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Many modern pharmaceutical medicines originally derive from compounds first identified in traditional plant based remedies, showing a direct, ongoing connection between traditional nonagricultural plant use, such as herbal medicine, and modern scientific medical research, similar to the connection between indigenous and modern industry explored in an earlier lesson in this strand.

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Create agricultural materials from different plant parts that are used to carry out agricultural activities.
- Create nonagricultural materials from different plant parts to carry out nonagricultural activities.

pages.title: From Knowledge to Practical Creation
pages.body: Lessons 13 and 14 built up detailed knowledge of the many agricultural and nonagricultural uses of plant roots, stems, leaves, flowers and fruits. This final lesson in the substrand, and in the entire Basic 9 course, focuses on actually creating simple materials or items from plant parts, turning that accumulated knowledge into a genuine, practical, hands on skill.

questions.q: This final lesson in the substrand mainly focuses on
o: Memorising more facts with no practical activity
Studying plant parts only in theory
Turning knowledge of plant part uses into hands on creation
questions.e: This final lesson in the substrand, and in the entire Basic 9 course, focuses on actually creating simple materials or items from plant parts, turning that accumulated knowledge into a genuine, practical, hands on skill.

pages.title: Creating a Simple Agricultural Material
pages.body: Preparing plant based compost from collected leaves, as studied in an earlier strand, weaving a simple plant fibre rope or twine useful for tying plants to stakes, or creating a small planting stick or dibber from a straight, sturdy stem are examples of simple agricultural materials that can realistically be created from plant parts using basic, accessible techniques and tools.

pages.title: Creating a Simple Nonagricultural Material
pages.body:
Weaving a simple basket or mat from palm fronds or grass, preparing a basic herbal tea from a recognised, safe medicinal leaf, under appropriate guidance, or carving a small decorative artefact from a dried fruit shell, such as a calabash, are examples of simple nonagricultural materials or items that can realistically be created from plant parts.

[[pic:A two panel illustration, the left panel labelled Creating an Agricultural Material showing a learner weaving plant fibre into simple twine for tying plants, and the right panel labelled Creating a Nonagricultural Material showing a learner weaving palm fronds into a simple basket, with materials and tools clearly visible in each panel.]]

Notice how both processes rely on similar hands on skills, careful selection and preparation of plant material, followed by shaping or weaving it into a useful final form, even though the resulting materials serve very different purposes, one agricultural and one nonagricultural.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Choosing Suitable, Safe Materials and Activities

pages.title: Choosing Suitable, Safe Materials and Activities
pages.body: Choosing plant parts that are genuinely safe to handle and, where relevant, safe to prepare as food or medicine, is an essential first consideration before beginning any practical activity in this lesson. Any activity involving preparing a plant part for consumption, such as an herbal tea, should only be attempted using a plant part positively identified as safe and edible, ideally under the guidance of a knowledgeable adult, since some plants can be toxic or cause allergic reactions if incorrectly identified or improperly prepared.

pages.title: Demonstrating and Explaining Your Created Material
pages.body: Once a simple agricultural or nonagricultural material has been created, demonstrating it to others and clearly explaining which plant part was used, how it was prepared, and what practical purpose the finished material serves, reinforces and communicates the full range of knowledge studied across this entire substrand, from identifying plant part uses in Lessons 13 and 14, to actually producing something useful from that knowledge in this final, practical lesson.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Small scale craft production based on plant materials, such as basket weaving, mat making, and rope production, remains an active source of income and cultural expression in many Ghanaian communities, meaning the practical skills introduced in this lesson connect directly to genuine, valuable traditional and small business activity, not simply a classroom exercise disconnected from real world application.
